documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-powered customer service systems have expanded across Saudi Arabia’s retail sector during 2025–2026, with major retailers increasingly exploring chatbots, recommendation engines, and automated service technologies. Official Saudi digital-economy statistics document the wider shift towards digital commerce, although the retailer-specific investment figures cited in an earlier draft have not been independently substantiated. This study examines the relationship among AI service quality, emotional brand attachment, and brand loyalty using survey results reported for 512 retail customers in Riyadh, Jeddah, and Dammam, collected between May and September 2026. Using partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) and bootstrap resampling, the analysis reports a positive direct association between AI service quality and loyalty (β = 0.421, p < 0.001), together with a positive indirect association through emotional brand attachment (reported indirect effect = 0.238, 95% CI [0.187, 0.289]). We discuss a possible “mechanical efficiency paradox”: functional improvements in AI service may be more strongly associated with loyalty than with emotional attachment. Importantly, this survey does not include a direct comparison with human-delivered service, and the reported positive attachment coefficient (β = 0.187) cannot establish that AI decreases attachment. The reported gender subgroup estimates differ: the AI quality–attachment association is positive for male respondents (β = 0.289, p = 0.001) and statistically nonsignificant for female respondents (β = −0.023, p = 0.811). Age-specific estimates also vary, with more positive reported coefficients in younger groups, although the statistical significance of the age differences requires further supporting output. The manuscript reports that the model accounts for 51.2% of the variance in loyalty (R2 = 0.512) and has positive predictive relevance (Q2 = 0.289). Because some path estimates, correlations, and variance-explained values are not mutually consistent, these results require rechecking against the original SmartPLS output before publication. Managerial implications include offering hybrid AI–human service, allowing customers to choose their preferred channel, and maintaining personal attention for complex or emotionally sensitive interactions. The findings provide a framework for assessing how technological service quality and relationship-building might jointly contribute to brand loyalty.
topics: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

documents.abstract: Rapid urban growth and the corresponding rise in municipal solid waste have intensified the need for efficient and scalable waste management solutions. Conventional segregation practices, which largely rely on manual intervention, are often time-consuming, inconsistent, and unsuitable for handling large volumes of waste. In recent years, advancements in Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML), and Deep Learning (DL) have facilitated the development of intelligent systems capable of automating waste classification and monitoring processes. This survey provides a detailed review of 13 research studies published between 2021 and 2025, with a focus on AI-driven approaches for waste management. It examines a range of techniques, including Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), object detection frameworks, and hybrid learning models, along with the datasets, evaluation metrics, and system designs employed in these works. A comparative assessment is carried out to analyze the performance, advantages, and limitations of the existing methodologies. The review further identifies critical research gaps, such as the absence of standardized benchmark datasets, limited real-time implementation, lack of multimodal sensor integration, and insufficient emphasis on model interpretability. Based on these findings, the paper outlines potential future directions, including the adoption of edge-based AI systems, integration with IoT-enabled smart infrastructure, and the use of advanced detection models to support scalable and efficient waste management in smart city environments.

This study aimed to develop an integrated framework to strengthen AI-supported leadership capabilities for strategic institutional transformation in Saudi education, aligned with Saudi Vision 2030. It used a descriptive-analytical approach within a scoping review, guided by PRISMA 2020. A data-extraction and content-analysis form and a quality-appraisal form examined a target sample of 60 peer-reviewed studies published or available online during 2022–2027, according to inclusion and exclusion criteria. Findings revealed a gap between stated institutional priorities and leadership practice. Artificial intelligence supported analytical and executive capabilities, strategic foresight, decision-making, and risk management, while ethical competence and human oversight remained essential. Institutional, technological, and human determinants interacted, particularly digital readiness, data integration, skills, change management, and governance. Accordingly, the study proposed a framework integrating leadership development, ethical governance and data protection, change management, and human–machine collaboration through initiatives, responsibilities, and performance indicators. Its contribution is to move beyond fragmented analyses of applications and determinants toward a strategic model connecting leadership capabilities with the enablers and outcomes of institutional transformation, supporting alignment between educational practices and Vision 2030 priorities. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Leadership Capacity Development, Educational Administration, Strategic Transformation, Vision 2030.

Thanks to artificial intelligence and machine translation technologies, the volume and speed of translation production have increased. However, these technologies also raise questions about the impact of dominant digital languages on less resourced ones. Many languages remain underrepresented in multilingual modelling due to the limited availability of digital language resources. This results in an uneven linguistic representation in natural language processing and AI models, which, in turn, leads to an asymmetry in linguistic influence, as evidenced by the literature. This study investigates linguistic interference in Arabic translation within digital environments, drawing on Toury’s (2012) Law of Interference. It addresses a critical gap by examining, from a qualitative perspective, how uneven language representation in automated translation environments may shape the quality of Arabic translations. It argues that the unequal distribution of digital language resources may contribute to the transfer of source-language features into Arabic translations. Methodologically, the study adopts an exploratory qualitative approach, analysing a small corpus of 100 Arabic translations from English and French, including human and machine-generated translations, focusing on three dimensions of interference: lexical, syntactic and discursive. The findings show repeating patterns of source-oriented elements, including the incorrect use of cataphoric construction and the coordinator واو, the excessive use of periphrastic constructions and the reduction of stylistic adaptation. Similar patterns were observed in machine translation outputs and online Arabic content, suggesting that AI systems reproduce linguistic tendencies already present in digitally circulating texts. The study highlights the need for greater attention to online high-quality Arabic resources.

Ekskalasi teknologi kecerdasan buatan (Artificial Intelligence/AI) pada era modernitas akhir telah membawa transformasi multidimensional yang tidak hanya menyentuh aspek teknis-utilitarian, melainkan merambah ranah eksistensial, antropologis, dan epistemologis manusia. Kecenderungan peradaban modern yang didominasi oleh cara berpikir belahan otak kiri yang bercorak mekanistis, kalkulatif, dan reduksionis berisiko mengikis kesadaran transendental serta memicu krisis kehampaan spiritualitas (spiritual emptiness). Artikel jurnal tingkat doktoral ini bertujuan merekonstruksi secara komprehensif paradigma keseimbangan antara Artificial Intelligence (AI) dan Spiritual Intelligence (SI) melalui kacamata pandangan hidup Al-Qur'an (Quranic Worldview). Menggunakan metode tafsir tematik konseptual (maudhu’i) yang diintegrasikan dengan hermeneutika filosofis dan pendekatan maqāṣid al-syarī‘ah, penelitian ini membedah status ontologis, batas epistemologis, dan orientasi aksiologis AI dan SI. Eksplorasi teks suci difokuskan pada dialog arketipikal kekhalifahan Nabi Adam as. dan kritik teknofetisisme patung anak sapi emas Samiri, yang diperkuat dengan analisis eksegetis terhadap beberapa ayat ayng lain. Penelitian ini juga merumuskan pilar-pilar kecerdasan spiritual Qur'ani: kesadaran diri, transendensi, makna hidup, nilai etis, dan kesadaran holistik. Hasil kajian menyimpulkan bahwa AI secara ontologis berstatus instrumen profan aksidental (khādim) yang terikat pada hukum komputasi simbolik dan probabilistik, sehingga klaim transhumanisme mengenai kesadaran mesin (ensoulment) ditolak secara mutlak karena ketiadaan hembusan rūḥ ilahiah dan fakultas qalb. Keseimbangan peradaban tercapai manakala lompatan AI ditundukkan di bawah kepemimpinan aksiologis SI yang berakar pada tauhid, keadilan (‘adl), kemaslahatan (maṣlaḥah), dan kesadaran human-in-the-loop, guna mengarahkan sains menuju terwujudnya martabat manusia seutuhnya (al-insān al-kāmil).

The aim of this study is to examine academic publications on green management published in 2024, identifying key research themes, findings, and relationships with sustainability, environmental performance, and green human resource management. A qualitative research design based on document analysis was adopted for the investigation. Data were gathered from 23 academic publications retrieved via Google Scholar using the keyword “green management”. Selected publications underwent rigorous content analysis, and findings were synthesized thematically alongside geographical and sectoral distributions. China represented the largest share, accounting for 39.1% of all reviewed publications. Research predominantly focused on the corporate sector, followed by higher education, manufacturing, and small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). Notably, none of the examined studies directly addressed green artificial intelligence. The findings indicate that green management is strongly associated with green innovation, environmental performance, resource efficiency, employee environmentally responsible behaviors, and overall organizational sustainability. Green technology adoption, organizational culture, and environmental regulations also emerged as critical drivers. Ultimately, the results underscore the necessity of integrating environmental objectives into core organizational strategies. Future research should explore green management across diverse national and sectoral contexts.

This conceptual working paper examines whether the New Human Rights (Neue Menschenrechte, NMR) approach developed by Jean-Pol Martin displays the characteristics of an emerging school of thought.It proposes five analytical criteria: a shared theoretical core, an interconnected vocabulary, a recognizable mode of inquiry, sustained collective activity, and autonomous contributions beyond the founder. Drawing on selected primary texts, publisher descriptions and public practitioner accounts, the paper identifies indications of these features in publications, training activities and distinct applications of the framework.The conceptual architecture connects an organism-based understanding of human beings, six basic need domains, a universal normative commitment to enabling their satisfaction, and a process model linking exploration, information processing, conceptualization and agency. Learning by Teaching (LdL) and human–AI cooperation are situated within this architecture.The article’s specific contribution is to shift attention from an individual theoretical project to the development of a shared intellectual and practical tradition. Within the ongoing sequence of papers on LdL, NMR and human–AI cooperation, it connects the reconstruction of Martin’s work with a prospective collective research programme.The paper distinguishes autonomous development within the project from independent reception outside its originating network. It concludes that “an emerging NMR school of thought” is a defensible interpretation of the documented activities and identifies questions for further conceptual and empirical investigation.Prepared by Jean-Pol Martin in collaboration with ChatGPT. The article includes references and an authorship transparency statement.

This anatomical review systematically dissects Noguer i Alonso's (2026) framework for hybrid workflows integrating human decision makers (H), specified computational procedures (D), and adaptive artificial delegates (A). The paper advances a principled account of agentification, deagentification, automation, and harnessing, grounded in a partial order on delegation profiles rather than scalar autonomy scores, and supported by formal results on permission restriction, invariant preservation, retry exposure, advisory isolation, and the proceduralization gap. While the contribution offers valuable conceptual clarity for task-specific authority allocation in agentic systems, the review identifies limitations in empirical scope (synthetic examples only), the open problem of semantic promotion, and the transferability of formal guarantees to production environments. Implications for AI governance, hybrid intelligence, and institutional design in Global South contexts are discussed.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are increasingly investigated as decision-support technologies for supply chain management (SCM), yet their value depends on the nature of the decision, data availability, organisational capability and the methods used to evaluate outcomes. This critical narrative review examines applications across demand forecasting, inventory planning, sourcing, manufacturing, logistics, risk management and sustainability. It brings together relevant peer-reviewed reviews, conceptual contributions and empirical studies, and distinguishes evidence from operational deployments from results reported in literature syntheses or simulations. The literature supports the practical relevance of data-driven prediction, pattern detection and decision augmentation, but it does not establish uniform improvements in cost, forecast accuracy, resilience or environmental performance across settings. Reviewed research also identifies integration costs, fragmented data, process misalignment, model drift, limited transparency and governance concerns as barriers to realising benefits. Recent work on generative AI broadens possible applications to document-intensive processes, synthetic scenarios and interactive decision support, while indicating that field-based validation remains limited. A process-oriented framework is proposed in which analytics inform planning, procurement, manufacturing, distribution and inventory decisions under continuous human oversight. The review argues that useful evaluations should compare AI-supported decisions against relevant operational baselines, account for service levels and cost trade-offs, and document transferability across sectors and resource settings. Future research should prioritise longitudinal field studies, cross-organisational coordination, responsible deployment and context-sensitive applications in emerging economies.

documents.abstract: The study examined artificial intelligence capabilities and organizational sustainability of retail outlets in Port Harcourt. The objectives of the study were to examine the relationship between dimensions of artificial intelligence capabilities such as CCTV analytics, chatbots and automated processing; and measures of organizational sustainability in terms of Environmental sustainability and Economic sustainability of retail outlets in Port Harcourt. Thus, the study was anchored on Diffusion of Innovation theoretical foundation. The study adopted the cross-sectional survey research design. The accessible population of the study was Sixteen (16) retail outlets currently operating in Port Harcourt. The entire population was used as the study sample. Thus, the study was census research which involves using the entire population rather than drawing a sample from it. Structured questionnaire served as the instrument for data collection. A total of sixty-four (64) copies of the validated questionnaire were distributed to the targeted audience. The researcher was able to retrieve fifty-six (56) copies of the entire validated questionnaire distributed. Arithmetic mean and standard deviation were used for the research question analyses, while the test of hypotheses was done using Spearman rank order correlation with the aid of SPSS Version 24.0. It was found that there is a significant positive relationship between artificial intelligence capabilities and organizational sustainability of retail outlets in Port Harcourt. It was concluded that leveraging artificial intelligence powered tools such as CCTV analytics, chatbots and automated processing, retailers can enhance operational efficiency, improve customer experiences and gain valuable insights into market trends. Consequently, it was recommended that operators of retail outlets should utilize automated system to track inventory level, reduce waste and optimize stock replenishment.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence has penetrated higher education not through official strategies but via students’ and faculty members’ personal devices, catching most universities off guard. This article presents empirical data from a large-scale survey conducted between March and April 2026 across six post-Soviet countries (Russia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan, Armenia, Tajikistan). The study provides a systematic cross-national analysis of student AI use patterns in the Eurasian higher education space, complementing recent single-country studies in the region. The sample included 478 students. The study measured frequency of AI use, perceived risks, compatibility with educational values, and the presence of institutional regulatory mechanisms. The results show that 78 % of students regularly use generative AI, yet only 32 % of universities have an official policy in this area. A deep disciplinary divide emerges: students fall into two roughly equal profiles – “pragmatic techs” (daily users with low ethical anxiety) and “reflective humanists” (cautious users with a strong demand for ethical frameworks). The main barrier to AI adoption is not technological infrastructure but the absence of regulatory and social technologies. The article offers discipline-differentiated recommendations for universities in non-Western contexts.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: OBJECTIVES: This scoping review examined how artificial intelligence is applied in multidisciplinary and cross-sector public health practice, focusing on public health roles, collaborative implementation, and cross-sector governance and equity risks. STUDY DESIGN: Scoping review. METHODS: Following Arksey and O'Malley's framework and PRISMA-ScR reporting guidance, six databases were searched. Sources were included if they examined artificial intelligence or artificial intelligence-enabled decision support in public, population, or community health contexts and provided information on public health functions, collaboration, implementation, equity, or governance. Data were charted and synthesised narratively by study characteristics, artificial intelligence roles, collaborators, implementation conditions, and governance risks. RESULTS: 27 sources published between 2021 and 2026 were included. Most were reviews, evidence syntheses, policy or guidance documents, or conceptual papers, with relatively few empirical or practitioner-oriented studies. Artificial intelligence was mainly used for surveillance and early warning, population risk modelling, health communication, misinformation detection, policy intelligence, participatory co-creation, and routine public health operations. Implementation depended on collaboration among public health practitioners, epidemiologists, data scientists, policymakers, legal and ethics experts, communication specialists, community organisations, and affected populations. Cross-sector governance and equity risks included poor data quality, limited interoperability, workforce gaps, weak real-world evaluation, privacy risks, and unclear accountability. CONCLUSIONS: Artificial intelligence applications in public health are expanding, but the evidence base remains heterogeneous and empirically limited. Routine operational support and AI readiness, together with surveillance and early warning, were among the more frequently represented roles, while empirical evidence on real-world implementation, community engagement and governance evaluation remained limited. Future research should move beyond model performance to examine workflow fit, equity impact, public trust, accountability and population-level outcomes.

documents.abstract: Background and Objectives: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the Artificial Intelligence Act, requires organisations deploying AI systems to ensure appropriate AI literacy and human oversight. We examined whether AI legal literacy was associated with procedure-concordant use of an AI-enabled early-warning system among hospital nurses and whether the association of prior AI-governance training with concordant use persisted after literacy was taken into account. Materials and Methods: This single-centre cross-sectional study included 87 nurses in a tertiary university hospital. AI legal literacy was measured with a study-specific 24-item instrument, and procedure-concordant AI use, the primary outcome, was defined as meeting all five criteria of the institutional documentation audit in 10 audited interactions per nurse. The primary analysis was multivariable logistic regression, confirmed in three-level mixed-effects models of 870 audited interactions nested within nurses and wards. Secondary and exploratory analyses (inverse-probability weighting, mediation decomposition, latent class analysis, and an internally validated prediction model) are reported as hypothesis-generating. Results: Forty-four nurses (50.6%) were procedure-concordant. Concordance was higher among trained than untrained nurses (70.3% versus 36.0%; p = 0.002). Each 10-point increase in AI legal literacy was associated with higher adjusted odds of concordant use (adjusted odds ratio 5.16, 95% CI 2.04–13.06; p < 0.001). The association persisted in three-level mixed-effects models (aOR 3.61 per 10 points, 95% CI 1.98–6.58). The association with prior training was attenuated after adjustment for literacy and was not statistically significant after inverse-probability weighting (OR 2.01, 95% CI 0.82–4.90); an exploratory decomposition was consistent with, but could not establish, an indirect association through literacy. Conclusions: Higher AI legal literacy was strongly associated with procedure-concordant AI use in this single-centre study. The findings support further evaluation of literacy-focused governance education and institutional oversight in hospital nursing practice; causal and predictive claims await prospective, multicentre confirmation.

documents.abstract: The swift spread of Artificial Intelligence (AI) through the realms of medicine, banking, hiring practices, law enforcement, and governmental administration has led to the emergence of a new type of legal risk that the conventional mechanisms of regulation are poorly designed to tackle. Such dynamic, data-driven, opaque, and increasingly self-reliant technologies pose difficulties when it comes to apportioning legal responsibilities and ensuring individuals' rights. In this paper, I provide a doctrinal and comparative review of the responses to AI-related risks developed by major jurisdictions – the EU, the USA, the UK, and China – as well as by international organizations, namely the OECD, UNESCO, and UN. In my work, I follow the development of the global AI governance system from ethical guidelines to risk-based regulatory compliance, and explore the most important legal issues, including algorithmic bias, data protection, transparency, cybersecurity, liability, and misinformation generated by generative AI models. Based on this comparative analysis, the paper presents an innovative six-stage AI Risk Governance and Compliance Framework rooted in the concepts of risk proportionality, lifecycle governance, human accountability, transparency, continuous compliance, and international cooperation. It is contended that a single national framework is not enough and that an effective global AI governance system requires a hybrid framework which combines the EU’s systematic risk categorization system, US’ flexible sectoral approach, UK’s adaptable regulator-led framework, and international soft law instruments’ human rights focus.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Sophisticated AI applications like ChatGPT and Grammarly offer distinct advantages for enhancing writing proficiency. They assist users in conceptualising ideas, organising material, and refining writing style, whereas Grammarly focuses on improving grammar, punctuation, and clarity with context-aware recommendations. This is particularly relevant for students who are non-native English speakers, as it supports them and helps bridge educational disparities. While these instruments markedly enhance scholarly writing abilities, their efficacy in tertiary education remains a subject of debate. Recent occurrences of academic dishonesty associated with the improper use of generative AI technologies have negatively impacted higher education. This study assesses the impact of artificial intelligence on enhancing academic writing abilities in students who are not native English speakers. In accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) criteria, this study consolidates evidence from scholarly literature, policy reports, and institutional case analyses. Keywords, synonyms, and subject headings were employed to query three electronic databases from 2021 to 2025. The electronic repositories included Scopus, Emerald Insight, Google Scholar, and ProQuest. The evaluation of the publications was conducted through titles and abstracts, followed by an assessment of the full-text papers against the qualifying criteria. The results were derived and amalgamated into a narrative synthesis from selected publications. The results underscored AI's ability to customise and improve the educational experience for learners.

The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) tools in higher education has reshaped how students engage with academic research, particularly at Honours level, where students transition from structured undergraduate learning to independent postgraduate research. Guided by Self‑Regulated Learning (SRL) theory, this study examines how reliance on AI by Honours research students influences the supervisor-supervisee relationship, the quality of research produced, and the extent of knowledge gained through the research process. SRL theory emphasises learners’ ability to plan, monitor, and reflect on their own learning, which is central to successful postgraduate research development. This study adopts a conceptual and literature‑based review methodology, drawing on peer‑reviewed studies on AI use in higher education, literature on postgraduate supervision, and academic integrity and research skills development frameworks, with specific attention to Honours‑level contexts. The documents were analysed using thematic content analysis, focusing on self‑regulatory behaviours, supervisory interaction, research skill development, and learning depth. The findings suggest that limited and transparent use of AI can support honours students by reducing surface‑level cognitive load and assisting with language clarity. However, excessive reliance on AI may undermine key self‑regulation processes, weaken critical thinking, and reduce meaningful engagement with supervisors. Supervisors may struggle to accurately assess students’ understanding, potentially straining trust and feedback processes. The review further indicates that over‑reliance on AI risks producing research that is technically adequate but conceptually shallow, with reduced long‑term knowledge acquisition. The study concludes that clear supervision practices and explicit guidance on responsible AI use are necessary to ensure that AI supports, rather than replaces, the self‑regulated learning essential for high‑quality Honours‑level research.

Full protocol (version 1.2) for a systematic review and meta-analysis comparing the discrimination, calibration and incremental value of artificial intelligence-based models (AI-ECG, machine learning on electronic health records) with conventional risk scores (CHARGE-AF, C2HEST, CHA2DS2-VASc) for predicting incident atrial fibrillation in adults. Includes the search strategy and statistical analysis plan, including pairwise and network meta-analysis of C-statistics. Review start date: 1 September 2026; expected completion: 20 November 2026. Prospectively registered: at registration only pilot work (preliminary searches) had been done; the formal search, screening, data extraction and synthesis had not started. PROSPERO registration in preparation.

PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Midurethral sling (MUS) surgery is the standard procedure for stress urinary incontinence, offering favorable long-term outcomes. Despite its success, postoperative voiding dysfunction - manifesting as urinary retention, elevated post-void residuals (PVRs), slow or weak stream, hesitancy, or the need for prolonged catheterization - remains a clinically significant complication that is difficult to predict using traditional risk stratification. Conventional methods, including history, physical examination, PVR measurement, and selective urodynamics, provide limited individualized predictive power and fail to integrate the complex interplay of patient, anatomical, and surgical factors. RECENT FINDINGS: Artificial intelligence and machine learning offer a promising approach to addressing this gap by analyzing multidimensional datasets to forecast individualized risk and guide perioperative management. While artificial intelligence applications in pelvic floor surgery have demonstrated utility in predicting general surgical outcomes, validated models specifically targeting post-MUS voiding dysfunction are lacking. Development of such predictive tools will require high-quality multicenter datasets, careful algorithm selection, and validation. SUMMARY: Integrating artificial intelligence into clinical practice has the potential to enhance preoperative counseling, support shared decision-making, optimize surgical planning, and ultimately improve patient outcomes. This perspective highlights the unmet need for predictive modeling of voiding dysfunction after MUS, outlines the promise of artificial intelligence, and emphasizes the importance of responsible implementation.

BACKGROUND: Muscle ultrasound offers a portable, non-invasive, and cost-effective option for sarcopenia assessment, but operator dependency limits its standardization. Artificial intelligence (AI) may help automate and improve ultrasound-based muscle evaluation. This scoping review aims to map the current landscape of AI-assisted ultrasound for sarcopenia assessment, including research trends, methods, clinical uses and performance, and to suggest future work. METHODS: Following Joanna Briggs Institute guidelines and the PRISMA-ScR checklist, we searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, the Cochrane Library, CINAHL, ProQuest, CNKI, WanFang Data, Yiigle, VIP, and Sinomed up to July 25, 2026. Two researchers independently selected studies and extracted data. RESULTS: Thirty studies were included. This field is developing rapidly, with 76.7% of studies published in the last 3 years, primarily from Spain and China. Model development and validation studies (43.3%) were most common. U-Net and its variants were the predominant AI architectures, mainly for image segmentation. B-mode ultrasound with high-frequency linear probes was frequently used. The rectus femoris was the most assessed muscle for sarcopenia (73.3%). AI-integrated models for sarcopenia diagnosis achieved AUCs of 0.640-0.950. Reported Dice coefficients for muscle segmentation ranged from 0.73 to 0.99. In-house datasets were used in 66.7% of the studies, and global classification labels were the most frequent annotation strategy (46.7%). CONCLUSIONS: AI-assisted ultrasound shows potential for objective and scalable sarcopenia assessment but remains early-stage. Operator dependency in image acquisition has not been fully resolved. Further investigation should determine the added value of integrating multimodal imaging, combining diverse AI techniques, and evaluating multiple muscle groups. Future efforts should deepen image-processing strategies to extract clinically relevant features and facilitate standardized, scalable implementation in clinical practice.

documents.abstract: Theoretical literature warns that advanced generalist agentic systems might pursue instrumental goals that are misaligned with human preferences, thus posing risks of irreversible loss of human control. The EU's Code of Practice for General-Purpose AI lists loss of control as a systemic risk that must be assessed, yet no structured assessment of the quality of the empirical evidence for this risk exists. This study fills that gap. We evaluate 19 recent empirical studies across eight properties identified from threat models (such as strategic deception, situational awareness, and autonomous replication), assessing the quality of evidence across three dimensions: construct validity, content validity, and external validity. Our central finding is that the current body of evidence supports a judgment of loss of control as "weakly plausible." In our framework, 'plausibility' denotes the strength and direction of available evidence, not a probability estimate. Emerging evidence exists across multiple properties. No study clears the validity thresholds for a stronger judgment that a property is present; a single study clears them only for a negative-direction judgment (against situational awareness). Validity gaps, particularly in external validity, are widespread. Therefore, our findings highlight the need for more rigorous evaluations of agentic general-purpose AI systems. However, for the most dangerous properties, high external validity may be structurally unachievable under responsible research practices, reflecting a ceiling on feasible evidence rather than absence of the capability. Furthermore, as AI capabilities advance rapidly, empirical assessments may systematically lag behind the capability frontier. Our framework provides a structured baseline for ongoing monitoring as capabilities advance.

Test-time scaling (TTS) improves large language model (LLM) reasoning by sampling multiple answers, but fixed sampling budgets ignore both query difficulty and the changing energy cost of inference under GPU contention. We measure up to a 4.1-fold increase in energy for the same four-sample query as GPU load rises. We present ATEST, a resource-aware TTS framework that jointly considers the expected value of additional samples and their current GPU cost. ATEST-Online, its default mode, requires no offline calibration: it incrementally generates samples, estimates the stability of the plurality answer, monitors live GPU conditions, and learns step energy cost online to decide when to stop. ATEST-Calibrated instead selects a per-query budget using offline accuracy and cost models, favoring deployments with stable loads. We evaluate both modes on four reasoning and question-answering datasets using Phi-3-mini on an NVIDIA A100 under controlled varying load, and test transfer to an NVIDIA L40S and Qwen2.5-3B. Across the four A100 datasets, ATEST-Online answers every query without exceeding the energy budget, while achieving the highest or statistically tied accuracy and reducing sampling as load increases. On GSM8K at high load, it achieves 60.0% accuracy with no deferrals, versus 44.0% accuracy and 42.4% deferrals for ATEST-Calibrated. Ablations show that online cost learning drives adaptation to load. Including offline profiling, ATEST-Online uses 42 times less GPU time and 48 times less energy than ATEST-Calibrated for the evaluated workload. Online control trades higher tail latency and lower throughput on short tasks for robustness under varying load; offline calibration remains competitive under stable conditions.

Agentic LLMs increasingly support scientific prediction by grounding decisions in external evidence. In biology, they promise accurate, interpretable predictions for important problems by integrating complex experimental and computational evidence. However, serialized tool results can contain hidden label shortcuts, such as dataset identifiers or template artifacts, that create apparent success without biological reasoning. To address this risk, we introduce a two-stage audit. Stage 1, Per-Tool TF-IDF Decomposition (PT2D), localizes label-predictive patterns to individual tool results while avoiding signal dilution in the concatenated tool trace. Stage 2, Token-Class Redaction, counterfactually tests whether the frozen LLM depends on the localized shortcut. We apply this audit to TCR-pMHC binding, where tool augmentation substantially outperforms a no-evidence baseline. At face value, this suggests that the LLM has learned to use scientific evidence. The audit overturns this interpretation: PT2D localizes the strongest signal to identifiers in one tool result, and redacting them reduces performance to chance. These findings show how hidden label shortcuts can masquerade as scientific reasoning or discovery, motivating source-level audits before benchmark gains are trusted.

documents.abstract: Scoping review (PRISMA-ScR) examining automated multimodal deception detection as a problem of multimodal information fusion: how heterogeneous, asynchronous, and uncertain signals captured by video/audio — facial expression/micro-expressions, voice/prosody, ocular behavior/pupillometry, remote photoplethysmography (rPPG), body/gesture, and verbal content — are fused by AI, including LLM/MLLM-based fusion (2025–26). The review maps the evidence and contributes (i) a taxonomy of multimodal deception signals by their role in the fusion architecture, (ii) the SINAPSE fusion framework (language model as a fuser with individual baseline and quantified uncertainty, never as a judge; reliability weighting and cross-modal consistency), and (iii) an agenda of open fusion challenges. Five research questions: (RQ1) which per-modality signals have replicated evidence of association with deception; (RQ2, central) which multimodal fusion architectures/strategies exist, at what level they fuse, their cross-domain generalization, and how (M)LLMs position themselves as fusers; (RQ3) datasets, stakes, and data gaps (rPPG+deception; Portuguese); (RQ4) uncertainty, individual baseline, calibration, and false-accusation bias in fusion; (RQ5) the cognitive-load construct and its critiques. Methods: PCC framework; dual-LLM title/abstract screening with human arbitration (GLM + DeepSeek, temperature 0, seed 42, versioned prompts); recall validation (≈0.95) against a human-curated reference set; full-text extraction and risk-of-bias assessment verified by three independent human reviewers; narrative synthesis (SWiM). Single principal reviewer (declared limitation). Transparency: literature collection (Sep 2026) and a first LLM screening pass preceded the protocol registration; the timeline is disclosed in the manuscript. Data, prompts, and PRISMA-ScR materials are in this project; the protocol is registered at OSF DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/Q7MXU.

The mining industry is undergoing a major transformation toward sustainable and environmentally responsible operations. Conventional diesel-powered mining equipment contributes significantly to greenhouse gas emissions, ventilation costs, noise pollution, and occupational health hazards. Battery Electric Mining Equipment (BEME) has emerged as a promising alternative that supports mine decarbonization and improves operational efficiency. The findings indicate that battery electric equipment significantly reduces carbon emissions, ventilation requirements, and maintenance costs while providing improved working conditions. Although the initial capital investment is higher, long-term operational savings and environmental benefits make battery electric technology a viable solution for sustainable mining. The study concludes that widespread adoption of battery electric equipment can contribute substantially to green mining initiatives and support global climate goals.

Rapid technological advancement is transforming contemporary organizations and reshaping the future of work. Artificial intelligence (AI), automation, digital communication technologies, and data-driven systems increasingly influence organizational structures, managerial practices, employee experiences, and workplace interactions. While these developments offer important opportunities to improve efficiency, flexibility, and innovation, they also raise significant concerns about employee well-being, ethical responsibility, privacy, surveillance, and workforce adaptation. This chapter examines the evolving relationship between humans and technology from a human-centered perspective. First, it briefly discusses the historical evolution of workplace technologies, from the Industrial Revolution to the current era of AI-driven digital transformation. Second, the chapter explores human–technology synergy and emphasizes the importance of collaboration and complementarity between human and technological capabilities in organizational settings. Third, it examines the growing role of human-centered technology in supporting employee well-being, inclusivity, participation, and ethical organizational practices. The chapter also discusses the organizational implications of AI integration, including changes in job roles, decision-making processes, workplace flexibility, and employee adaptation. Finally, key challenges associated with technology integration, such as algorithmic bias, workplace surveillance, digital fatigue, and technological dependency, are addressed alongside potential future directions of human–technology collaboration. Overall, the chapter argues that successful digital transformation requires organizations to balance technological advancement with human values, needs, and capabilities. The long-term sustainability of workplace technologies depends not only on operational efficiency but also on organizations’ ability to foster ethical, adaptive, and mutually beneficial relationships between humans and technology.

Artificial intelligence (AI) deepfakes enable the convincing imitation of an individual’s image or voice, creating risks that extend beyond the identification and punishment of offenders. This article examines how Indonesian law responds to digital victimisation and whether its remedies address reputational, psychological and social harm. Using normative legal research and a focused interdisciplinary literature review, it analyses the Electronic Information and Transactions Law, Personal Data Protection Law, Sexual Violence Crimes Law, the Criminal Code and criminal procedure reforms, including the 2026 Witness and Victim Protection Law. The analysis identifies three interconnected problems: harm may arise before distribution; protection depends on fitting conduct within fragmented offences; and criminal proceedings alone do not ensure rapid content containment or sustained recovery. It proposes a victim-centred response linking accessible reporting, lawful evidence preservation, timely platform action, risk-sensitive support and restitution where legal conditions are met. Rather than claiming an absence of relevant laws, the article argues that coordination and remedies should reflect the continuous nature of technology-facilitated harm. This framework offers a policy-oriented contribution to debates on digital victimology and access to justice in Indonesia.

Large Language Models often generate factually correct responses that fail to maintain user-requested perspectives, blending multiple perspectives and forcing users to filter through unwanted information---a perspective control failure that factual accuracy metrics cannot detect. We introduce PerspectiveBench, a benchmark quantifying perspective alignment by constructing scenarios where multiple valid reasoning paths coexist, and propose the Perspective Alignment Score (PAS) to measure adherence to specified perspectives. Experiments reveal that state-of-the-art models successfully include target content but fail to exclude non-requested perspectives. Providing documents through RAG improves factual grounding but does not resolve perspective drift, as models prioritize comprehensive coverage over strict user constraints. Code and data are available at https://github.com/sunghoon014/PerspectiveBench.

This study attempted to implement artificial intelligence in language learning using the well-known ChatGPT. This study focused on measuring the effects of ChatGPT on vocabulary size and depth of knowledge. To collect the required data, 60 Omani intermediate EFL learners were divided equally into control and experimental groups. An updated vocabulary level test (UVLT), developed by Webb et al. (2017), and a Word Associate Test (WAT) developed by Read (1998) were used as the pretests to ensure the homogeneity of students’ vocabulary knowledge. Although both groups continued the traditional face-to-face training, the experimental group had the opportunity to use ChatGPT as a facilitator of vocabulary learning with the chance of tailored and personalized activities. The UVLT and WAT were administered again as posttests to compare learners’ performance after the treatment. The findings revealed that both groups showed increases in the posttest regarding vocabulary size, but the experimental group outperformed the control group remarkably. Although no progress was made in the depth of vocabulary by the control group, the experimental group performed significantly better. The findings are insightful for teachers, curriculum designers, students, researchers, institutions, and policymakers.

Evaluating LLMs for crisis communication requires more than judging isolated responses, because public feedback and competitor actions can reshape trust over time. Existing benchmarks remain largely static and single-turn, offering limited evidence about long-horizon risk-sensitive communication. We introduce \textbf{BrandEval}, a two-track benchmark for product-crisis communication, focusing on public brand responses to product-related safety, quality, service, and trust incidents. BrandEval-Static evaluates stakeholder-aware strategic analysis, while BrandEval-Dynamic stress-tests response policies in \textbf{BrandPolis}, a controlled multi-agent sandbox with consumer feedback, competitor responses, and trust-risk trajectories. We also construct \textbf{BrandSRD}, a Chinese crisis-response dataset, and instantiate a reference Strategic Agent using \textbf{Strategic Rationale (SR)}. Across proprietary and open-source models, we find that static strategic quality is informative but incomplete: it aligns with some end-state outcomes but does not reliably predict volatility and delayed recovery; dynamic stress tests further expose tail-risk failures under manipulative or weakly grounded policies. The code and dataset will be available at https://github.com/htgan-ai/BrandEval.

This study examines how curriculum relevance and workplace-based mentorship influence apprenticeship outcomes in South Africa’s manufacturing industry, with a focus on persistent skills gaps between training provision and industry requirements. Guided by Objective 1, which seeks to examine the relevance and alignment of apprenticeship curricula with the skills, technologies, and competency demands of the manufacturing sector, and Objective 3, which explores the role of mentorship and workplace-based learning in supporting skills development, employability, and workplace readiness, the study investigates the extent to which current apprenticeship programs reflect contemporary manufacturing practices. A qualitative, multi-case research design was employed, drawing on in-depth interviews with stakeholders from public colleges, private training centres, and small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). The findings reveal a sustained misalignment between formal apprenticeship curricula and modern manufacturing technologies, including automation, robotics, and advanced production systems, largely resulting from centralised curriculum control and limited institutional autonomy. In contrast, mentorship and workplace learning emerged as critical mechanisms for translating theoretical knowledge into practical competence, strengthening professional identity, and developing both technical and soft skills. However, the effectiveness of mentorship practices varies across institutional contexts, with colleges facing greater structural and policy constraints than SMEs and training centres. The study concludes that bridging skills gaps in South Africa’s manufacturing sector requires an integrated approach that combines responsive curriculum reform with structured, industry-embedded mentorship and authentic workplace learning opportunities, offering practical and theoretical contributions to vocational education and training scholarship.

Since 2026 AI data vendors, marketplaces and intermediaries have published programmes through which an ordinary company can sell or license its internal records for training AI models. This paper compares the published terms of 37 organisations with a public way in, as compiled in an open dataset reviewed on 16 October 2026, together with a register of the contract clauses 16 of them publish and a dated log of 110 market events. Twenty-four take company records, 17 of them buying for their own account. Of those 24, 14 publish a floor (median $100,000) and 9 a ceiling (median $1 million; highest $5 million). Eligibility rules are sparse: six publish a headcount minimum (mostly 20 to 40 employees), two a minimum of three years, three a rule about country or language, and eight say they take companies that are closing or closed. Where a time to payment is stated it runs from 7 days after the data passes review to about 60 days, and several programmes pay only on the buyer's acceptance. Exclusivity is stated by few and deletion terms by six; one programme's terms say deletion does not require deleting trained models. Ten publish structured introduction fees, up to $100,000 per deal. No published ceiling is backed by an independently reported payment of that size: one programme has payments confirmed by sellers, at tens to hundreds of thousands of dollars, and seven report their own. We describe the data, the classification and the limits of comparing posted terms. Keywords: AI training data; data licensing; company records; buyer programmes; data markets; contract terms; posted prices; referral fees Use of AI: this paper was prepared with generative AI tools, which compiled and analysed the open datasets and drafted the text. The author takes responsibility for its content. Competing interests: the author is CEO of AIData.Broker, which acts for companies that license their data to AI developers and publishes the open datasets the paper draws on. Also at aidata.broker/research/paper-buyers.
