documents.abstract: Reasoning large language models (LLMs) benefit from test-time scaling, motivating adaptive policies that spend tokens when they help and stop early otherwise. Existing rules halt when a confidence or stability signal crosses a threshold, but such thresholds rarely transfer across models and datasets, and validation-calibrated rules lose their guarantee under shifts in test-time horizon or signal dynamics. We reframe adaptive stopping as sequential evidence accumulation along the reasoning trajectory rather than threshold calibration on held-out data. Our framework runs two e-processes on a shared per-chunk signal: a commit stream tracks the signal's position relative to its slow trend, and an abstain stream tracks its signed velocity, making the two anti-correlated by construction. Under signal-level nulls on the per-chunk increments, Ville's inequality yields an anytime-valid signal-level false-alarm bound at user-specified significance levels, with no held-out calibration. Across various model--dataset combinations, the framework matches or exceeds calibration-based stopping on the token--accuracy Pareto front using zero calibration data, and the same significance level transfers unchanged across cells where calibration becomes infeasible.

The rapid emergence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in social media has introduced Artificial Influencers as a new form of digitally constructed endorser, challenging conventional assumptions about authenticity, trust, and consumer behaviour. Unlike human influencers, Artificial Influencers are technologically created personas whose appearance, personality, communication, and interactions can be deliberately designed and controlled. This raises an important question: Can consumers perceive an Artificial Influencer as authentic when they are aware of its artificial nature? The present study examines the role of AI disclosure in shaping perceived authenticity and explores how authenticity relates to consumer trust and purchase intention in the context of social commerce. The study specifically addresses an emerging authenticity–trust–purchase intention paradox, whereby consumers may recognise an influencer as artificial, perceive limitations in its authenticity, and nevertheless remain willing to trust its recommendations or consider purchasing promoted products. A quantitative, exploratory, and cross-sectional research design was adopted. Primary data were collected through a structured online questionnaire from 30 social-media users using non-probability convenience sampling. The questionnaire examined respondents’ social-media exposure, awareness of Artificial Influencers, perceptions of AI disclosure, perceived authenticity, consumer trust, and purchase intention. Frequency and percentage analysis were used to describe response patterns, while Spearman’s rank-order correlation was employed to examine associations among the principal constructs. Given the small sample size, the study is positioned as an exploratory investigation and does not seek to establish population-level generalisation or definitive causal relationships. The findings indicate that AI disclosure has a dual significance in consumer evaluation. While 73.3% of respondents supported AI disclosure always or in most cases, disclosure was also associated with increased scrutiny of recommendations and greater concerns regarding genuineness. At the same time, 73.3% of respondents indicated that an Artificial Influencer could be perceived as authentic under certain circumstances, particularly when communication was relatable and consistent. However, 70.0% reported that awareness of AI generation reduced their perception of authenticity to some degree. Consumer trust appeared to be conditional rather than automatic, with respondents emphasising transparency, credibility, consistency, product relevance, and information verification. Purchase intention was similarly cautious, with respondents indicating that willingness to purchase depended on the product and the credibility of the recommendation. The study concludes that artificiality and authenticity should not be treated as mutually exclusive concepts. Consumers may simultaneously recognise the technological construction of an Artificial Influencer, experience reduced perceptions of genuineness, and still regard the influencer as sufficiently credible to support trust and purchase consideration. The findings therefore provide preliminary support for the authenticity–trust–purchase intention paradox and suggest that AI disclosure functions not simply as a mechanism that reduces authenticity, but as a transparency cue that can coexist with scepticism. The study contributes to the emerging literature on AI-mediated influencer marketing by integrating AI disclosure, perceived authenticity, consumer trust, and purchase intention within a single exploratory framework. For marketers, the findings highlight the importance of transparent disclosure, credible and verifiable product information, consistent communication, and responsible consumer engagement when deploying Artificial Influencers in social commerce.
topics: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

documents.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is a promising way to improve the clinical reasoning abilities of large language models (LLMs), but current pipelines often rely on expert-labeled questions or costly synthetic-data generation. Meanwhile, the medical literature offers a wealth of high-quality unlabeled documents, including clinical case reports that trace the full clinical course from initial presentation to final treatment decisions. We study whether document-grounded self-play can convert these reports into effective RL training signals. We identify two challenges that limit existing self-play methods in this setting: knowledge-point fixation}, where the proposer repeatedly asks about a narrow set of salient clues in a source report, and difficulty-quality mismatch, where appropriately difficult questions may still be poorly formed or shallow, limiting their value for reasoner training. To address these challenges, we propose CasePlay, a self-play framework with two key components: (a) a Knowledge-Conditioned Proposer, which anchors question generation to case-specific knowledge points so that questions draw on a broader range of evidence from the source report; and (b) a Rubric-Judge Reasoner, which augments answer-accuracy feedback with rubric-based quality feedback on clue integration, reasoning depth, and option quality, guiding the proposer toward reasoning-intensive questions that better support reasoner training. Extensive experiments across seven medically related benchmarks demonstrate that CasePlay outperforms existing self-play baselines and improves the SFT warm-start model by 3.1 points on average, highlighted by a 6.3-point gain on LiveClin. This approach offers an effective path toward continually improving medical reasoning ability through self-play RL.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Offline sepsis treatment aims to learn treatment policies from retrospective ICU trajectories. Decision Transformer-based methods provide a natural sequence modeling framework for this task, but they mainly rely on raw physiological states and historical clinician actions. Such raw trajectory tokens may not explicitly capture clinical semantics that clinicians use in practice, such as patient severity, recent treatment response, and current risk priorities. To address this limitation, we propose ClinSDT, an LLM-assisted Decision Transformer framework for offline sepsis treatment. ClinSDT uses a frozen LLM as a semantic bridge rather than a treatment decision maker. It constructs three clinical semantic views from ICU trajectories, namely Profile, Context, and Advisory, and inserts their encoded representations as independent tokens into a Decision Transformer policy. To support policy refinement and rollout, ClinSDT further trains a Treatment-Response Forecaster to estimate the next physiological state, SAPS-II change, and predictive uncertainty from state-action inputs. In the second training stage, the forecaster screens local counterfactual treatment candidates, and only low-uncertainty candidates with lower predicted SAPS-II increase are distilled into the policy after semantic regeneration. During inference, ClinSDT performs closed-loop treatment rollout by refreshing semantic inputs from the currently available patient state. Experiments on MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV show that ClinSDT achieves consistent relative improvements over representative imitation learning, offline reinforcement learning, and Decision Transformer baselines under the same rollout protocol. Code and data are available at https://github.com/KAG778/ClinSDT.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Commercial crab fishing involves physically demanding tasks that increase the risk of work-related musculoskeletal disorders. This study evaluated fishermen’s perceptions of occupational exoskeletons as a potential intervention to reduce physical demands in commercial fishing. Twenty commercial crab fishermen completed an in-person survey after trying soft and/or rigid exoskeletons. The survey assessed fishermen’s demographics and work characteristics, awareness, adoption and acceptance factors, potential applications, and perceived barriers to exoskeleton use. Descriptive statistics and content analysis were used to summarize responses. Fishermen identified practicality as the key adoption factor and shared concerns about cost, time required to don and doff the device, bulkiness, and incompatibility with rain gear. Crab pot handling and crab sorting were identified as potential use cases. Overall, fishermen viewed exoskeletons as potentially useful for reducing physical demands during commercial crabbing; however, successful adoption will require lightweight, comfortable, and affordable designs compatible with fishing gear and challenging work conditions.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being integrated into healthcare education and clinical decision-support systems. While ChatGPT has demonstrated promising performance in medical and dental domains, comparative evidence regarding newer models such as DeepSeek remains limited, particularly in oral pathology. This pilot study aimed to compare the performance of ChatGPT and DeepSeek in oral pathology education and evidence-based diagnostic decision support. We conducted a cross-sectional comparative study from January to December 2025. We developed ten oral pathology educational questions and five standardised clinical case scenarios based on established dental curricula and authoritative oral pathology references. Identical prompts were submitted independently to ChatGPT and DeepSeek. Responses were anonymised and evaluated by three board-certified oral pathologists using a structured rubric assessing accuracy, completeness, clinical relevance, diagnostic reasoning, and evidence-based consistency. Each domain was scored on a 5-point Likert scale, with a maximum total score of 25. Statistical analyses included independent-samples t-tests, Cohen’s d effect sizes, and intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) assessment. ChatGPT achieved a significantly higher mean total composite score than DeepSeek (23.2 ± 1.8 vs. 20.6 ± 2.4; p = 0.006; Cohen’s d = 1.15). ChatGPT also outperformed DeepSeek across all evaluation domains, including accuracy (4.72 ± 0.31 vs. 4.18 ± 0.52; p = 0.003), completeness (4.68 ± 0.37 vs. 4.10 ± 0.55; p = 0.005), clinical relevance (4.61 ± 0.42 vs. 4.09 ± 0.58; p = 0.011), diagnostic reasoning (4.58 ± 0.46 vs. 3.98 ± 0.63; p = 0.008), and evidence-based consistency (4.75 ± 0.29 vs. 4.16 ± 0.49; p = 0.002). Large effect sizes were observed across all domains. Inter-rater reliability demonstrated excellent agreement among evaluators (ICC = 0.87; 95% CI: 0.81–0.92). ChatGPT demonstrated superior performance compared with DeepSeek in oral pathology education and evidence-based diagnostic decision support. Its higher accuracy, completeness, clinical relevance, and consistency with established evidence suggest considerable potential as an adjunctive educational and clinical support tool. Nevertheless, human oversight remains essential to ensure accuracy and mitigate the risks associated with AI-generated outputs. Further large-scale studies incorporating real clinical cases and multimodal diagnostic data are warranted.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: We compare three AI services, TypeSafe Jev (jev-1.13.0), the OpenAI Decisions API (gpt-6-luna) and Claude Haiku 5.5 (claude-haiku-5-5), as assistants for title and abstract screening in literature reviews. Each service sees a record's title, abstract, keywords, year and venue with the review's coded eligibility criteria, and suggests advance, exclude or unsure. Suggestions are compared with human screening decisions in four to six reviews from the SYNERGY dataset and, separately, in one review screened in SLReviewFlow. The primary outcome is recall of human inclusions, with a bar of 0.95 on every dataset. Secondary outcomes are work saved, precision, specificity, kappa, criterion agreement, unsure rate, output validity, stability, cost and latency. Thresholds and wording are tuned on a random half of each dataset; all headline results come from the other half. Reporting follows RAISE 2 and the TRIPOD-LLM checklist.

Health systems are deploying large language models (LLMs) into clinical workflows, often on the assumption that a second automated check can only reduce error. But a second reasoner reduces error only insofar as it fails differently from the first. We say that a clinician and a model have complementary vulnerabilities to the extent that they break down through different mechanisms and on different cases. The two reasoners' failure substrates differ: they are embodied and cognitive in the clinician, and statistical and generative in the model - so their weak points need not line up. That divergence is plausible rather than guaranteed, and the independence it creates is fragile, eroding when clinicians defer to the model or the model conforms to the clinician. We therefore propose a predeployment audit in which each site measures error overlap on its own cases. We also propose a governance model with which the site keeps those errors independent over time. Health systems should then judge a clinical artificial intelligence (AI) tool by whether its failures overlap with their clinicians' failures, as well as by its accuracy.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Despite the significant contribution of HAIs to increased morbidity, mortality, length of hospital stay, and escalating health care costs, they continue to be a major public health problem globally.New and fast spreading "MDROs" (Multidrug Resistant Pathogens) including MRSA (Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus), VRE (Vancomycin-resistant Enterococci), ESBL (Extended-spectrum β-lactamase) producing Enterobacteriaceae, CRE (carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae), Acinetobacter baumannii and Pseudomonas aeruginosa have further contributed to the complexity of infection management in hospital settings.Due to the various resistance mechanisms such as enzymatic degradation, induction of efflux pumps, alteration of permeability and biofilm formation, there are limited therapeutic options and poor clinical outcomes available for these pathogens.This systematic review will assess the effectiveness of complete hospital infection control with an emphasis on infection prevention and control (IPC) interventions, surveillance tools and antimicrobial stewardship programs (ASPs).The standard and transmission based precautions, environmental hygiene and device associated IPC bundles (CLABSI, CAUTI, VAP) are critical reviewed as basic IPC approaches.The use of advanced surveillance tools, such as Electronic Health Records (EHR) surveillance, Microbiological antibiogram development, and AIdriven predictive analytics for early detection and outbreak management are also discussed.In addition, the effect of antimicrobial stewardship interventions (formulary restriction, de-escalation, pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) optimization, and WHO AWaRe classification integration) on trends in antimicrobial resistance and hospital outcomes are evaluated.Future tools for infection control that are emerging as a result of research are noted as being artificial intelligence, quick molecular diagnostics, and nanotechnology antimicrobial surfaces.However, there are still challenges to be addressed, such as the improper use of antibiotics, limited resources, and non-compliance with treatment by health personnel.It exposes the need for multi-disciplinary, integrated approaches that include IPC, surveillance, and stewardship to effectively support the fight against MDR pathogens and patient safety in health care systems worldwide.

Before a clinical encounter even formally begins, we neurologists watch a foot hesitate at a doorway, a stride shorten on the way to the chair, a subtle change in facial animation during a greeting. We watch for amplitude, speed, asymmetry, overflow, and the countless combinations thereof. We watch in the clinic, in corridors, sometimes as early as the waiting room. This observation fills many of our working hours. And yet, for all the advances in molecular imaging, genetics, fluid biomarkers and artificial intelligence, Parkinson’s disease is still often first recognised through this language of movement - in what the body does, how it does it, and what it no longer quite does. Video has long been part of this practice, helping us teach, document, compare and remember 1 . In their recent editorial in Brain , Ganos, Stanley and Lang argue that video in movement disorders is never just a recording – it is what shapes clinical representation, pedagogy and the visual norms through which human variation is understood. As such, it carries scientific value, but also moral weight: it documents disease, and it documents a person living with it 2 . Artificial intelligence has now arrived at the core of this visual tradition, offering tools that can document and measure movement from an ordinary video, including smartphone recordings, without expensive, complex hardware. Not long ago, this would have seemed an audacious prospect for a field so intimately linked to visual documentation. With the advent of convolutional neural networks, it has become a reality. Computer vision promises to take what neurologists already do – carefully observe movement - and make it measurable, repeatable, and available beyond clinic walls and the constraints of tight schedules. In Parkinson’s disease, this is an attractive proposition: a disease that fluctuates over hours and days, and evolves over years, is still assessed largely through brief, artificial clinical encounters. We ask patients how they have been over weeks or months, then score a few minutes of performance under fluorescent lights, often at a time of day that may not represent their usual function - not to mention the “good day effect”. We know this practice is born of a lack of better tools, and that it is insufficient. Our patients know it too. The literature gives reason for optimism. Recent reviews show that Parkinson’s disease is the most frequently studied movement disorder in computer vision research, that gait is the most common task and that diagnostic accuracies frequently exceed 80% 3 . Open-source and commercial platforms suggest the field is moving from bespoke engineering demonstrations toward shared clinical tools 4 . Several studies, many published in npj Parkinson’s Disease , have further shown that computer vision may inform both clinical decision-making and pathophysiological investigation of parkinsonian bradykinesia across body parts, therapy conditions and care settings 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 . Beyond bradykinesia, computer vision has enabled video-based quantification of tremor amplitude and frequency, the pull test and facial expressivity, often with close agreement to reference methods such as motion capture and accelerometry 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 . A camera in a clinic, home or aged-care facility, it seems, could soon reveal meaningful motor information without wires, markers or specialist hardware 3 , 14 , 15 . Yet the growing number of publications should not be confused with equivalent progress towards clinically valid digital biomarkers. Showing that an algorithm can distinguish patients from controls, reproduce a clinical score or perform well within a selected dataset is an important first step, but it is not sufficient. A video-derived measure intended for clinical use must undergo the same scrutiny as any other biomarker or clinical outcome measure: it should demonstrate test–retest reliability, acceptable measurement error, construct validity, responsiveness to clinically meaningful change and robustness across populations, recording environments and disease stages. Crucially, we need to understand whether a change in the output reflects a true change in the patient rather than variation in camera position, lighting, task execution or model performance. Without this deeper clinimetric work, technical accuracy can easily be mistaken for biological or clinical validity. This may be a reason why the field has produced many models and feasibility demonstrations, but comparatively few, if any, clinically mature digital biomarkers. For all our fascination with these technological advances, and our desire to see them succeed, their potential is clear: better measurement, earlier detection, remote care, trial enrichment and more equitable access to specialist assessment. But realising that potential depends on addressing a pressing challenge: the translation of technical performance into valid measurement, clinical action and patient benefit. Beyond practical issues such as who requests, analyses and interprets video outputs, harder questions follow. A 10% change in finger-tapping amplitude means little until we know what it means for someone’s daily life. Increasing sensitivity may also shift the boundaries of what we call “prodromal” or “pre-symptomatic”, raising questions about disclosure, follow-up, responsibility and reimbursement. Patients must be involved in deciding how they feel about being filmed for diagnosis or monitoring. And any tangible benefit must be legible to both patients and their physicians, not just to a model. These are the implementation questions that separate a research instrument from a clinical tool. Addressing them will require implementation science from the outset, including evaluation of acceptability, feasibility, workflow fit, equity, sustainability and unintended consequences across diverse care settings. For selected motor tasks and recording conditions, the question is no longer simply whether computer vision can extract accurate measures of parkinsonian movement. Increasingly, we know that it can. The more relevant question is whether it can also become useful and valuable . A tool may be technically accurate and still be clinically irrelevant. It may correlate with a rating scale but fail to change a decision. It may add measurement without adding meaning. With the broad availability of wearable technology, medicine is generating a growing number of digital outcomes. Yet despite their technical validity, adoption in clinical studies and guidelines is very limited 16 , 17 . For computer vision to avoid this fate, it must be built around defined clinical decisions and care pathways rather than computational possibility, with explainability taking centre stage. Explainability should be treated not as a cosmetic layer added after model development but as a clinical requirement test with its intended users. Parkinson’s care does not need more numbers in the abstract. It needs help with practical, complex questions - questions such as “Is levodopa still helping?”, “Is gait changing because of Parkinson’s disease, arthritis, cognition, pain or environment?” and “Is this treatment effect large enough to matter to the person living with the disease”? There are harder questions still. If a computer vision algorithm detects deterioration before the patient does, but no effective intervention or care response is available, have we actually helped? Do patients even want this? If a model flags early Parkinson’s disease in someone not yet diagnosed, who carries responsibility for that knowledge? The ethical risks extend beyond the misuse of video data. They include the danger that patients become increasingly visible to health systems without becoming meaningfully better supported by them. Surveillance without response is not care. If a system can detect falls risk, wearing-off, freezing or deterioration, it must be connected to a pathway for timely action. Without such a pathway, computer vision risks becoming a sophisticated way of exposing disease-related need, while leaving that need unmet. This shifts the scientific goalposts away from technical benchmarks, bespoke coding-intensive solutions and clinically meaningless error metrics, and towards deployable, user-friendly and interpretable tools that generate outcomes of value to both doctors and patients. The value of such digital biomarkers extends beyond technical performance: it emerges from rigorous testing against the decisions and outcomes they are intended to inform. This aligns with the broader digital biomarker literature in Parkinson’s disease, which emphasises that digital measures require evidence of reliability, validity, interpretability, regulatory readiness and integration into care pathways before they can become clinically useful biomarkers 18 . More speculatively, computer vision can also inspire us to reconsider how we visually assess our patients. If computer vision can quantify a clinical gesture such as finger tapping - traditionally just a proxy for disease severity - with this much nuance, should we not leverage that precision to measure real-world function directly, i.e. moving towards “ecologically valid neuroscience”? Or, what if a machine’s attention could teach our own, by pointing our eyes to the regions of a video frame it found most informative for a given clinical outcome? 19 In both scenarios, explainability is paramount. Clinicians are more likely to trust and act on outputs that resemble clinical reasoning than “black-box” abstraction: a report visualising reduced amplitude, progressive decrement and increasing irregularity during finger tapping is more interpretable and likely more acceptable than an opaque probability derived from a model that clinicians struggle to understand, let alone explain to a patient. Such explanation must also be faithful to how the model reached its conclusion, rather than merely plausible visualisations generated after the event. The goal is not to replace the neurologist’s eye but to extend it - to slow it down, render it more quantitative and objective, and let it attend to moments it might have missed. This is the “discerning eye of computer vision”. Future directions for computer vision should therefore be ambitious, but not naive. We can imagine movement vital signs: brief standardised videos captured at home or before clinic, summarising gait speed, turning, arm swing or facial expressivity. We can imagine remote specialist augmentation, which rural clinicians, aged-care staff or general neurologists capture structured video and receive an interpretable, clinically governed movement summary - not a diagnosis from a machine, but a better map for human care. Other fields that have already travelled this path already offer us important lessons too. Radiology did not become digital simply because images could be processed; it built PACS, reporting standards, accreditation, quality assurance and clinical governance. Diabetes care did not integrate continuous glucose monitoring merely because glucose could be measured continuously; it became useful when patients, clinicians, devices, reimbursement systems and therapeutic algorithms converged around action. Aviation and other high-stakes contexts emphasise that automation becomes safe when embedded in systems that account for human behaviour, fatigue, error, accountability and trust. In this vein, we argue that the movement disorders field now needs its own infrastructure for visual, measurement-based medicine. That infrastructure must include not only technical standards, but implementation frameworks capable of identifying where, for whom and under what conditions computer vision adds value. The next phase of computer vision in Parkinson’s disease should be defined not by the number of movements that can be extracted from video, but by the number of video-derived measures that withstand rigorous biomarker validation and improve a specified clinical decision. That demands three things. First, standards: consensus protocols for video acquisition, metadata, reporting and validation. Second, proof: prospective implementation studies testing whether computer vision changes clinical decisions, outcomes or patient experience, with outputs co-designed with clinicians, patients and carers, not just delivered to them. Third, governance: bias and failure-mode audits, regulatory and reimbursement pathways matched to real use cases, and explicit responsibility when systems fail or performance deteriorates. Across all three, explainability should be evaluated empirically: can intended user understand an output, recognise its uncertainty and determine what action, if any, should follow? Publication standards should rise accordingly: retrospective performance in a curated dataset should be considered an entry point, not an endpoint. Priority should shift toward studies establishing whether a computer vision-derived measure is reliable, responsive, reproducible, generalisable and clinically actionable. Still, the most important future may be quieter than this: could computer vision help patients feel believed? Many people with Parkinson’s describe changes that are intermittent, subtle or hard to name. They know when walking has become subjectively less automatic, buttoning a shirt feels harder or medication subtly starts to wear off. A sensitive visual tool could make these experiences visible - not replacing the patient’s narrative, but standing alongside it. The measure of computer vision will not be merely its tracking accuracy, but whether it leaves the person in front of us better cared for - and, perhaps, better believed. Now comes the harder work: making computer vision part of medicine, not merely part of research. Just as Parkinson’s disease alters movement in fractions, with a little less amplitude and a little more effort, computer vision allows us to measure those fractions earlier, more sensitively and more faithfully. As a community of clinicians, scientists and people with lived experience, we must now decide what this new way of seeing is for. Its future will be determined not by how precisely algorithms quantify movement, but by whether those measurements improve decisions, transform outcomes, and ultimately, help people with Parkinson’s disease live better lives.

documents.abstract: Reinforcement learning improves the reasoning capability of large language models through verifiable rewards for mathematical and coding tasks. In token-level methods such as GRPO, clipping acts on individual token ratios while the reward and advantage apply to a complete response. Recent sequence-level methods align these units but still use fixed clipping bands, whose tail probabilities change as the score distribution evolves. We propose Conformal Prediction-Enabled Sequence-level Policy Optimization (CSPO), which adaptively calibrates sequence-level clipping bounds using recent training statistics. The resulting band targets a specified marginal tail budget and adapts to policy drift; calibration conditional on response length requires additional assumptions. We bound the probability that a fresh score falls outside the band by the target miscoverage level plus explicit CDF discrepancy and drift terms. Under additional moment conditions, this bound also controls the objective and gradient error relative to the unclipped GSPO power surrogate. Experiments with the Qwen3-1.7B series show improvements over GSPO on difficult mathematical reasoning benchmarks and ALFWorld, with clipping endpoints that adapt during training.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become increasingly integrated into educational, professional, and technological environments, creating opportunities for innovation while raising concerns regarding transparency, accountability, ethical responsibility, privacy, and governance. Despite the growing use of AI-powered technologies among university students, limited research has examined how engineering students perceive corporate governance practices associated with these technologies. This study explored the perceptions of undergraduate engineering students regarding corporate governance in AI-powered technologies. A descriptive quantitative research design employing a cross-sectional survey approach was utilized. Data were collected from ninety-two (92) undergraduate engineering students at Cebu Institute of Technology–University (CIT-University) using a structured questionnaire. Frequency counts, percentages, weighted means, and ranking procedures were used to analyze the data. The findings revealed that respondents demonstrated positive awareness of corporate governance principles in AI systems, particularly regarding ethical responsibility, accountability, transparency, and data governance. The respondents also expressed a generally favorable level of trust in organizations utilizing AI-powered technologies, although concerns regarding privacy protection, data security, and responsible AI implementation remained evident. Among the governance dimensions examined, accountability received the highest rating, followed by ethical governance and transparency. Furthermore, the results showed that engineering students generally practiced responsible AI use, particularly in avoiding technologies that violate ethical and privacy standards. Large Language Models (LLMs), such as Gemini, ChatGPT, and Claude, were identified as the most commonly used AI-powered technologies among the respondents. The study concludes that engineering students recognize the importance of responsible AI governance and view accountability, ethical responsibility, and transparency as essential components of trustworthy AI systems. These findings may contribute to the development of governance policies, educational initiatives, and responsible AI practices within academic and technological environments.

documents.abstract: Purpose This study investigates the micro-level structural differences in online review affect between social media and e-commerce platforms, exploring the underlying psychological mechanisms that drive consumers to selectively express polarised reviews across these media. Design/methodology/approach Utilising large language model-driven aspect-based sentiment analysis, this study quantifies an initial dataset of 65,493 smartphone online reviews from TikTok, Bilibili, Jingdong and Suning to identify aspect-level affective differences. To explain the observed differences, Study 2 draws on uses and gratifications theory and conducts a 2 × 2 between-subjects experiment, using wireless headphones as the focal product and TikTok and Taobao as the platforms, to examine how media environments moderate the translation of consumption experiences into review intentions. Findings Affective differences extend to specific cognitive attributes, with social media platforms exhibiting a significantly more negative and heterogeneous affective landscape, whereas e-commerce platforms demonstrate overwhelming positivity. These differences are driven by a dual-pathway mechanism. Social media platforms primarily activate self-enhancement motivation, which facilitates the translation of negative experiences into negative reviews while weakening the translation of positive experiences into positive reviews. Conversely, e-commerce platforms primarily activate economic motivation, which facilitates the translation of positive experiences into positive reviews while reducing the likelihood of negative experiences translating into negative reviews. Originality/value This study extends the investigation of review affect from within-medium comparisons to cross-media analysis. By shifting from macro-level indicators to micro-level attribute evidence, this study reveals a more comprehensive picture of cross-media affective bias. By extending the application of uses and gratifications theory from content consumption to content production, it offers a novel mechanistic explanation for this phenomenon.

Abstract: The availability of customer data, the advance of artificial intelligence (AI) and the growing importance of digital content and influencers have changed the tools that firms can use to increase sales. This narrative review examines how these three levers—data and analytics, AI-enabled personalization, and content and influencer marketing—contribute to sales growth, and under which conditions they generate results. Peer-reviewed studies and reference works published up to 2023 were analyzed qualitatively. The literature indicates that marketing analytics improves decisions on targeting, pricing and resource allocation; that AI supports personalization at scale, from mechanical automation to analytical and feeling-oriented applications; and that content and influencer marketing build engagement, trust and purchase intention when they are relevant and credible. Generative AI, which gained prominence in 2023, expands content production and customer interaction capabilities but also raises concerns regarding accuracy, transparency and ethics. The review concludes that these levers produce the greatest effect when combined in an integrated system in which data informs content and personalization, and results are measured and fed back into decisions. It also emphasizes that privacy, trust and human judgment remain essential conditions for sustainable sales growth.

Company records such as chat workspaces, mailboxes, documents and tables are proposed as training data for language models, and they carry identifiers of employees, customers and other organisations. This report describes a rule-based de-identification engine that runs entirely in the data holder's browser, so that raw records, the people learned from them and the key behind every pseudonym stay on the holder's computer. It combines the people an export names in its own structure, pattern detectors validated by check digits, cues and a public-domain name lexicon, and the holder's own lists. It writes stand-ins from a keyed HMAC-SHA-256, scoped to each file by default, holds every table row to a group of at least 11, screens content for special categories, and rereads its output with a second check that has no memory of the first pass. On the held-out split of the Text Anonymization Benchmark (127 court judgments) it masks every mention of 93.4% of direct identifiers. On the six human-annotated exports of PrivacyBench v2.5, not inspected while the rules were written, it reaches 86.8% F1 (precision 88.1%, recall 85.6%) using export structure, and 81.9% F1 on text alone. It is weakest on organisation names (49.9% recall), links (61.9%), account numbers (68.3%) and street addresses (87.4%). We report the protocol, the published comparison table and the threats to validity. Keywords: de-identification; pseudonymisation; personally identifiable information; named entity recognition; workplace data; k-anonymity; privacy engineering; training data; benchmark Use of AI: this paper was prepared with generative AI tools, which compiled and analysed the open datasets and drafted the text. The clinical success of immunotherapies is hindered by the absence of robust methodologies for the early and accurate assessment of antitumor immune responses. Integrating engineered biomaterials with artificial intelligence (AI)-driven molecular imaging technology offers a powerful approach for predicting immune efficacy. However, its clinical translation is significantly hindered by several critical limitations, including the complex and costly synthesis of multifunctional imaging probes, insufficient deep-tissue penetration, suboptimal in vivo signal-to-noise ratios, potential immunogenicity and off-target toxicity, and the limited generalizability of deep learning models across heterogeneous patient populations. In view of these pressing scientific challenges, this review focuses on the application of chemical and biomolecular strategies-enhanced engineered biomaterials in promoting the sensitivity and specificity of advanced imaging modalities for visualizing signaling molecules and immune cells in the tumor microenvironment (TME). Meanwhile, recent progress in deep learning-driven image analysis has enabled strong predictive capabilities and automated the understanding of complex immune system dynamics. Together, these technologies provide a transformative platform for non-invasive monitoring, personalized treatment, and response prediction, with the potential to advance precision immuno-oncology and significantly impact both basic research and clinical translation.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are characterized by having more than one principal element, in contrast to a traditional alloy with only one base element; this provides a much wider composition space compared to traditional alloys; hence, HEAs have been the most studied metal alloys in the last couple of decades. This review links the fundamentals of these materials to the data-driven methods now used to design them. The first part of this review describes the fundamentals of these materials, including the thermodynamic and kinetic basis of these materials and an entropy-based classification. The subsequent parts of this review describe the synthesis routes of these materials via liquid-state, solid-state, gas-state, and other processing routes. The choice of processing route can have a significant impact on the resulting material, including the phase(s) formed, the chemical homogeneity, and contamination of the material. We have systematically reviewed the mechanical, corrosion, thermal, electrical, and soft magnetic properties of these HEAs. In the final section, we discuss how artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) can be used to solve the problem of combinatorial explosion of the design space of HEAs: supervised classifiers for phase prediction, regression and ensemble models for hardness, strength, and elastic moduli, active learning and Bayesian optimization for closed-loop discovery, high-throughput screening with CALPHAD, and machine-learned interatomic potentials. We conclude with continuing constraints such as lack of data, noisy labels, and poor encoding of process history, and areas of development including transfer learning, generative design, and self-driving laboratories.

Enterprise systems are now often spread across a range of hidden technical and organizational dependencies; technical debt can accumulate, configurations can change, and failures can propagate. Redundancy or post-incident recovery alone is not enough for resilience design; such environments require continuously updated dependency knowledge and credible impact analysis before, during, and after change. This review considers peer-reviewed journal literature published between 2015 and 2024 that is relevant to the dependency mapping and impact analysis of resilient enterprise systems using AI. The studies included in the review are grouped around microservice architecture, process mining, digital twins, graph learning, anomaly detection, explainable artificial intelligence and resilience measurement, as well as AIOps. Based on the literature, it is shown that AI-based mapping can increase observability of runtime relations, aid in change-risk prioritization, and aid in failure localization with architectural models and operational telemetry. There are still gaps in causal validation, cross-layer dependency representation, data quality, explainability and evaluation against real enterprise incidents. There is scholarly value in the field, as resilient design increasingly relies on dynamic, evidence-based knowledge of how enterprise elements behave under stress, change and degradation.

Large-scale conversational recommendation datasets typically require manual dialogue construction or annotation. We propose SearCl, which automatically generates conversational recommendation dialogues grounded in user search and click behaviors. SearCl segments user interactions into query sessions and derives each recommendation target from content selected after a search query. A configurable probabilistic state machine controls the dialogue flow, while two LLM agents acting as the seeker and recommender generate utterances according to turn-level constraints. To support recommendation, the recommender is provided with knowledge graphs constructed from metadata about the content items used in each dialogue, capturing their attributes and relationships. Using SearCl, we generate 3,538 dialogues from content search and click interaction data, covering 1,731 unique target items. Under an LLM-as-a-judge protocol, the resulting dialogues achieve higher quality scores than dialogues from existing benchmarks. These results demonstrate that SearCl enables controllable and knowledge-grounded dataset construction without human annotations.

How well can transformer-based Large Language Models (LLMs) retain and recall memories in long contexts of dialogue? LLMs are known to forget long-range factual information in their context, yet the field lacks a comprehensive benchmark to quantitatively assess these shortcomings. We present DiaLong, a long-context dialogue dataset and accompanying memory task that standardizes evaluation in this space. It consists of 100 unique conversations created by humans and then augmented with LLMs, extending beyond lengths found in existing datasets. Our selected memory task is fact recall: classify 40 candidate facts about a dialogue as true or false. This task directly probes the model's ability to actively retain and retrieve information, serving as a critical measure of memory within extended conversational contexts. In testing both the latest LLMs and proposed memory enhancements on DiaLong, we demonstrate that more work needs to be done to enable LLMs with better memory performance. By enhancing memory capabilities, LLMs can improve in maintaining coherence, relevance, and human-like interaction over extended conversation. Improving these capabilities will help LLMs fulfill diverse user needs and expectations in various conversational scenarios.

Deutsch Dieses Konzeptpapier aus dem Jahr 2023 stellt einen Ansatz zur Demokratisierung künstlicher Intelligenz vor. Ziel ist die Entwicklung einer künstlichen demokratischen Intelligenz, deren Entscheidungsgrundlagen und Verhaltensregeln durch einen strukturierten demokratischen Dialog mit Menschen bestimmt und fortlaufend überprüft werden. Das Konzept beruht auf vier Demokratieaxiomen sowie den menschlichen Grundwerten Glück, Selbstbestimmtheit und Freiheit. Es unterscheidet zwischen Mikro-, Meso-, Makro- und Meta-Ebenen menschlicher Interaktion und entwickelt daraus eine sogenannte „Innere Direktive“ für künstliche Intelligenz. Im Mittelpunkt steht ein mehrstufiger demokratischer Dialogprozess, in dem eine KI als Moderatorin unterschiedliche Positionen zusammenführt, Kompromisse erarbeitet, Abstimmungen organisiert und Entscheidungen einer wiederkehrenden Evaluation unterzieht. Der Ansatz soll insbesondere verhindern, dass Mehrheitsentscheidungen grundlegende Interessen von Minderheiten verletzen. Anhand der Personalisierung von KI-Assistenten wird der vorgeschlagene Prozess exemplarisch dargestellt. Autor: Arnold Pohn-DudaOriginalfassung: 17. Juni 2023DOI: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23452894 English This concept paper, originally written in 2023, presents an approach to the democratization of artificial intelligence. Its objective is to develop a form of democratic artificial intelligence whose decision-making principles and behavioral rules are established and continuously reviewed through a structured democratic dialogue with humans. The concept is based on four axioms of democracy and the fundamental human values of happiness, self-determination, and freedom. It distinguishes between micro-, meso-, macro-, and meta-levels of human interaction and derives an “Internal Directive” for artificial intelligence. At its core is a multi-stage democratic dialogue process in which AI acts as a moderator, brings together opposing perspectives, facilitates compromises, organizes voting, and subjects decisions to recurring evaluation. The approach aims, in particular, to prevent majority decisions from violating the fundamental interests of minorities. The proposed process is illustrated through an example involving the personalization of AI assistants. documents.abstract: The digital economy has become a central component of contemporary economic transformation, but its contribution to growth is neither automatic nor evenly distributed. This article examines the principal channels through which digitalization can influence economic growth and synthesizes recent global evidence on productivity, innovation, employment, human capital, infrastructure, and institutional readiness. The study adopts a structured narrative-review approach drawing on established economic literature, recent peer-reviewed studies, and international policy reports. Three research questions guide the analysis: through which mechanisms does digitalization affect economic growth; why do growth effects differ across countries, firms, and sectors; and which policy conditions are most important for converting digital adoption into inclusive and sustainable economic gains? The review finds that digital technologies can raise productivity by lowering transaction and coordination costs, improving information use, enabling automation, expanding market access, and accelerating innovation. However, recent evidence also shows that productivity effects may be heterogeneous and nonlinear, particularly where firms lack complementary organizational capabilities, skills, finance, or absorptive capacity. Digital infrastructure and broadband remain foundational, while human capital and digital skills determine the extent to which firms and workers can exploit technological opportunities. Artificial intelligence, cloud computing, data analytics, and digital platforms are likely to strengthen these channels but may also intensify labor-market adjustment, market concentration, cybersecurity risks, and digital inequality. The article proposes an integrated policy framework centered on infrastructure, diffusion, skills, innovation capacity, institutional quality, and inclusion. It concludes that digitalization should be understood as a complementary-capabilities process rather than a stand-alone technological shock: long-term growth depends on how effectively digital technologies are combined with human capital, organizational change, competition, and responsive public policy.

Digital pedagogy has become an essential component of higher education, offering new opportunities to develop students’ critical thinking, analytical reasoning, problem-solving, and independent learning skills. This article examines how digital learning environments and technology-enhanced teaching strategies can support the development of critical thinking among university students. Particular attention is given to blended learning, problem-based learning, collaborative digital platforms, and artificial intelligence. The discussion draws on existing research and identifies practical approaches for integrating digital tools into higher education. The article argues that technology alone does not guarantee improved learning outcomes; effective digital pedagogy requires purposeful instructional design, active student participation, and continuous feedback.

In this paper, we investigate the issue of difference awareness in LLMs, defined as a model's ability to recognize and acknowledge meaningful differences between social groups in fairness decision-making. Previous studies have consistently shown that models perform poorly on such tasks, a finding commonly attributed to a lack of difference awareness. We propose an alternative account, which we term Fairness Heuristic Substitution: difference awareness is not necessarily absent, but the complex demand of simultaneously identifying relevant group differences and determining their implications for fairness decisions may lead models to substitute the simpler, more accessible equal-treatment heuristic, i.e., formal equality. Based on this hypothesis, we introduce TDD, a Two-stage Distinguish-Decide framework that explicitly decomposes fairness reasoning into first distinguishing contextually relevant group differences and then making the corresponding decision, thereby discouraging reliance on formal-equality shortcuts. (i) Across four benchmarks and ten models ranging from billions to trillions of parameters, TDD significantly outperforms one-stage baselines, even one strengthened through simulated test-set leakage. (ii) Combining TDD with neuron-level contrastive probing provides mechanistic evidence consistent with the Fairness Heuristic Substitution hypothesis by revealing two signatures of the formal-equality: a compact, locally coordinated representational structure and a pronounced activation bias under default reasoning. (iii) TDD's stage-wise decomposition uncovers overlooked failure modes in fairness reasoning, including heuristic displacement and misaligned stage dynamics.

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are often used to simulate survey respondents, but matching survey averages does not establish accurate demographic differences. We test whether LLM outputs reproduce within-country age gaps in loneliness using the 2022 EU Loneliness Survey, comparing adults aged 18-34 and 65 or older in France, Italy, Poland, and Sweden. We evaluate simulation with and without age information and direct distribution estimation against a probability-based sample, with a non-probability sensitivity reference. Both human samples show higher mean loneliness among younger adults. Under age-specified simulation with standard response-option order, Mistral Small 4 and GPT-5.6 Terra reverse this ordering under all three prompt framings in three and two countries, respectively, mainly by overestimating older-adult means. DeepSeek V4 Flash preserves the ordering everywhere but underestimates both group means, with errors largely cancelling in France and Italy. Against the probability-based reference, direct estimation has lower absolute age-gap error than simulation for Mistral and Terra in every country. For DeepSeek, simulation has lower gap error but direct estimation has lower group-mean error; these comparisons depend on low-validity older-adult simulation cells. Evaluating LLM outputs as proxies for age groups within countries therefore requires checking both group means and their contrast against human survey data.

documents.abstract: An AI agent can reproduce the distribution of its messages and of the receiver's task outcomes while disclosing private information that the task never required. We ask what a passive audit can certify when the auditor knows the authorised sender and the exact observable law but has no trusted pairing of messages with the private states behind them. For a single round, compatible mutual-information leakage forms a sharp interval, and fixing the entire task-relevant message law, with every declared task utility, can still leave a full private bit undetermined; total leakage is determined if and only if, in every task state, the remaining private state or the authorised message is a deterministic function of that state. For a sender, such as an LLM, that selects among its own responses, we prove that in a balanced case its change to the message law within each task state equals $(1-2^{-k})$ times the honest messages' dependence on the attribute, which also sets, up to a constant, how many messages a monitor needs. With Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct on a synthetic routing task, selection among 16 responses lets a public decoder recover a private bit in all 8,192 held-out rounds at 98.60\% routing accuracy (honest sender 98.90\%). A monitor that knows the selection rule reaches AUC 0.645 on single messages, close to the ceiling of 0.671 that honest messages predict, and 0.972 over 16, while generic monitors stay near chance. A law-preserving sender built from the same samples recovers the bit in 97.7\% of rounds, and every monitor without the true bit stays near chance against it. A canonical task interface preserves every receiver decision and bounds the remaining information about a balanced attribute by twice the routing-error rate, even for a receiver that shares a key with the sender. These results distinguish what passive auditing can certify from what restricting communication can enforce.

documents.abstract: Scientific foundation models increasingly operate on continuous phenomena, yet still use discrete residual computation. We ask whether pretrained residual transformations can support additional latent computation without expanding the backbone. To test this possibility, we introduce Continuum-LM, which reuses these transformations as dynamical operators in a continuous-depth language model. Its hidden states evolve through an ordinary differential equation evaluated by higher-order numerical integration, with solver order and step size controlling computation. Across eight scientific tasks, Continuum-LM trains stably and improves mean exact-match accuracy by 7.77 and 10.96 percentage points over discrete counterparts at the 0.6B and 1.7B scales, respectively. At 0.6B, it also outperforms an Ouro-style recurrent control under matched parameter and residual-function evaluation budgets. Together, these results support extensible computational depth through parameter reuse, identifying continuous hidden-state evolution as a practical design dimension for scientific language models beyond parameter scaling.

AI agents that provide interpretable messages can support clearer communication between humans and automated systems in situations where drivers need to respond within a few seconds. However, the potential of these capabilities to assist drivers during the takeover process remains unknown. Therefore, this study examined the effects of AI roles, explanation type, and directional semantics in speech-based takeover requests on takeover performance, as measured by decision quality (decision-making time and accuracy), and on subjective ratings. Twenty-four participants took part in a within-subjects SAE Level 3 driving simulator study. Among the three AI roles, Advisor AI was associated with faster decision-making times, and Guardian AI was associated with a lower workload. Co-Pilot AI was associated with the slowest decision-making times, lower accuracy, lower trust than Advisor AI, higher anxiety than Guardian AI, the lowest satisfaction, and the highest workload. The ipsilateral display was associated with shorter decision-making times than the contralateral display. Overall, the findings inform the integration of AI into next-generation automated systems.

LLM-based search agents demonstrate strong capabilities in long-horizon information seeking and reasoning, typically trained via reinforcement learning. However, existing approaches predominantly rely on trajectory-level outcome rewards, providing limited supervision for complex search and reasoning processes. Although step-level credit assignment offers a promising solution, obtaining reliable and task-grounded supervision for open-ended search remains challenging. In this paper, we propose Evidence-Guided Group Relative Policy Optimization (EG-GRPO), a framework that derives step-level supervision from the evidence annotations available in synthetic deep search data. EG-GRPO identifies the first supporting citation for each required evidence claim and uses the newly acquired evidence to construct step-level process rewards. By representing the accumulated evidence as an evolving knowledge state, EG-GRPO further performs state-conditioned relative advantage estimation and combines the resulting step-level signal with the standard trajectory-level outcome advantage. Experiments on five challenging deep search benchmarks show that EG-GRPO generally outperforms standard GRPO and existing reward-enhanced and step-level RL baselines across different model scales. These results demonstrate that task-grounded evidence annotations can provide effective process supervision for credit assignment in deep search RL.

Falls from heights remain a leading cause of fatal workplace accidents, with psychological stress contributing to human error. Electrodermal activity (EDA) and heart rate (HR) are promising stress markers whose real-world, physically demanding applicability remains underexplored. This study examined whether EDA and HR discriminate stress responses between certified and basically trained firefighters, and how these responses evolve across task phases. Seventeen male firefighters from the Moravian-Silesian Region, Czech Republic, completed an ascent, tower-top stay, and rappel from a 50-meter industrial cooling tower. EDA was recorded at the wrist and lumbar region using Sensetio wearable sensors, and HR via a Polar H10+ chest strap. After visual inspection, SCL was extracted from EDA; SCL and HR were both resampled to 600 samples (200 per phase) and min–max normalized. Functional data analysis using point-wise Mann–Whitney U tests, complemented by a cluster-based permutation test for multiple comparisons, compared SCL and HR between groups. SCL increased in both groups, but novices showed an earlier, steeper rise during the ascent and tower-top phases, forming two significant clusters after permutation correction ( t ≈ 59 –213, p c l u s t e r = 0.026 ; t ≈ 219 –421, p c l u s t e r = 0.017 ) with large effect sizes (median r = 0.71 ), whereas certified firefighters showed marked increases mainly during rappelling, where the difference narrowed and lost significance (median r = 0.46 ). No significant between-group HR differences emerged. Normalized SCL trajectories thus captured experience-related timing differences that HR did not, suggesting EDA warrants further investigation as a complement to safety training and monitoring, rather than as a validated readiness or error-risk-prediction tool at this stage.

documents.abstract: The growing population of stray animals presents pressing ethical and public concerns. We present an extended iStrayPaws, a Virtual Reality Perspective-Taking (VRPT) system combining first-person animal embodiment, shelter narratives, and a virtual behavioral assessment. In a longitudinal study, 48 university students were randomly assigned to VRPT, matched Desktop Perspective-Taking (DPT), or no-intervention Control conditions. State and trait empathy, animal-welfare attitudes, virtual-task performance, and attention were assessed before, immediately after, and one week after intervention. Significant Group × Time interactions emerged across all outcomes (ηp2=.12–0.21). Both VRPT and DPT improved empathy immediately, while VRPT additionally improved task performance and attention. At follow-up, VRPT retained advantages over Control in empathy, welfare attitudes, and task performance, and exceeded DPT in trait-empathy change and task performance. Greater presence was associated with immediate state empathy. Interviews indicated stronger narrative recall, emotional resonance, and welfare-oriented reflection in VRPT. Findings support immersive perspective-taking for sustained cross-species empathy and animal-welfare education.

The health and wellness of employees is now a focal point for companies aiming to optimize employee performance, build robust organizational performance, and ensure sustainable results. This systematic review aims to explore the connection between staff wellbeing and organisational performance, focusing on interventions in the workplace, implementation and outcomes. The review draws together the findings of literature on various interventions, such as the mental health support programs, flexible working arrangements, employee assistance programs, occupational health and safety interventions, leadership development, work–life balance policies, and employee involvement in organizational decision making. The results show that interventions at work that emphasize the psychological, physical and social wellness of workers can benefit job satisfaction, employee engagement, productivity, organizational commitment and retention. The review also emphasizes the need for ‘positive organisational culture', supportive leadership, ‘manageable workloads' and psychologically safe working environments to enhance the effectiveness of well-being strategies. But factors including lack of financial support, poor managerial support, stigma, uneven implementation, and measuring long-term effects may reduce their impact. Contextual factors, such as organizational size, industry attributes, employment conditions, and workforce diversity also play a role in the link between employee well-being and organizational performance. The review concludes that the wellbeing of employees should not be seen as a standalone human resource responsibility, but as a part of the strategy of the organisation. It suggests implementing workplace interventions that are evidence-based, based on inclusiveness, and continually assessed, balancing employee needs and organizational goals. The learnings from these insights are valuable in helping to build a broader picture of how employee well-being programs can contribute to sustainable performance and help managers, HR, and organizational policy makers better guide their employees.

Cirrhosis is a form of Chronic Liver Disease (CLD) resulting from sustained liver damage from several causes, including viral infection, autoimmune disorders, cholestatic and metabolic disease Non-Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (NAFLD) or heavy alcohol use. Testing for the presence of Liver Cirrhosis (LC) is one of the most critical diagnostics and prognostic assessments for patients. Detecting liver illness in its early stages is challenging as initial symptoms are often mild and difficult to diagnose. Cirrhosis may not present symptoms until an advanced stage, posing a challenge for identification and diagnosis. The lack of explanations for a complex model’s decision-making process creates clinician distrust by concealing the reasoning behind its choices. This research sought to design and assess a novel and non-invasive proposed model by utilizing the XGBoost classifier with Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) for diagnosing liver cirrhosis. In this work XAI framework enhances transparency in complex models, offering valuable insights into decision-making, thereby guiding treatment strategies, and improving cirrhosis diagnosis. The experimental results have shown superiority for the proposed method compared with various machine learning models. The proposed method has achieved significantly 91.19% using XGBoost for cirrhosis dataset with K-fold validation(K=10) approach.
